title: Integration
description: Antiderivatives, indefinite integrals, definite integrals, Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, area under and between curves, substitution, and kinematics.

notes.heading: Antiderivatives and Indefinite Integrals
notes.body:
Integration is the reverse process of differentiation. If you know the derivative of a function, integration lets you recover the original function.

📌 Definition
If $F'(x) = f(x)$, then $F(x)$ is called an antiderivative of $f(x)$.

The indefinite integral includes an arbitrary constant because any constant disappears during differentiation:
    $$\int f(x) \, dx = F(x) + C$$
    where $C$ is the constant of integration

🔑 Power Rule
For any rational number $n 
eq -1$:
    $$\int x^n \, dx = \dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} + C$$

💡 Worked Example — Using the Power Rule
Find $\int (6x^2 - 4x + 3) \, dx$.

  Step 1: Integrate each term separately
    $\int 6x^2 \, dx = 6 \cdot \dfrac{x^3}{3} = 2x^3$
    $\int -4x \, dx = -4 \cdot \dfrac{x^2}{2} = -2x^2$
    $\int 3 \, dx = 3x$

  Step 2: Add the constant of integration
    Result: $2x^3 - 2x^2 + 3x + C$

🔑 Standard Integrals You Must Know
    $$\int e^x \, dx = e^x + C$$
    $$\int \dfrac{1}{x} \, dx = \ln|x| + C$$
    $$\int \sin x \, dx = -\cos x + C$$
    $$\int \cos x \, dx = \sin x + C$$
    $$\int \sec^2 x \, dx = 	an x + C$$

💡 Worked Example — Finding the Constant of Integration
Given $f'(x) = 6x^2 - 4x$ and $f(1) = 3$, find $f(x)$.

  Step 1: Integrate to find the general form
    $f(x) = \int (6x^2 - 4x) \, dx$
    $f(x) = 2x^3 - 2x^2 + C$

  Step 2: Use the given point to find $C$
    $f(1) = 3$
    $2(1)^3 - 2(1)^2 + C = 3$
    $2 - 2 + C = 3$
    $C = 3$

  Step 3: Write the final answer
    $f(x) = 2x^3 - 2x^2 + 3$

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Always include $+C$ for indefinite integrals
• The power rule fails when $n = -1$ (use $\ln|x|$ instead)
• Integrating a sum means integrating each term separately
• A constant factor can be pulled outside the integral

⚠️ Common Mistake
Forgetting the constant of integration. If a question gives you a point on the curve and you omit $+C$, you will get the wrong answer. Every indefinite integral has infinitely many solutions — the $+C$ captures all of them.

notes.heading: Definite Integrals and FTC
notes.body:
While indefinite integrals give families of functions, definite integrals produce a single number. They are the tool we use to calculate exact areas.

📌 The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (FTC)
If $F'(x) = f(x)$, then:
    $$\int_{a}^{b} f(x) \, dx = F(b) - F(a)$$

The notation $[F(x)]_{a}^{b}$ means you evaluate $F$ at the top limit and subtract $F$ at the bottom limit.

💡 Worked Example — Evaluating a Definite Integral
Evaluate $\int_{0}^{2} (3x^2 + 1) \, dx$.

  Step 1: Find the antiderivative
    $F(x) = x^3 + x$

  Step 2: Apply the FTC
    $[x^3 + x]_{0}^{2}$
    $= (2^3 + 2) - (0^3 + 0)$
    $= 8 + 2 - 0$
    $= 10$

🔑 Area Under a Curve
When $f(x)$ is above the $x$-axis on $[a, b]$:
    $$	ext{Area} = \int_{a}^{b} f(x) \, dx$$

When $f(x)$ dips below the $x$-axis, the definite integral gives a negative value for that portion. Area must be positive, so you need to split the integral at the zeros and take absolute values.

💡 Worked Example — Area with a Curve Below the Axis
Find the total area enclosed by $y = x^2 - 2x$ and the $x$-axis.

  Step 1: Find where the curve cuts the $x$-axis
    $x^2 - 2x = 0$
    $x(x - 2) = 0$
    $x = 0$ or $x = 2$

  Step 2: Determine which function is on top
    On $[0, 2]$, the curve is below the axis, so $y_U = 0$ and $y_L = x^2 - 2x$

  Step 3: Set up the integral
    $$	ext{Area} = \int_{0}^{2} [0 - (x^2 - 2x)] \, dx$$
    $$= \int_{0}^{2} (2x - x^2) \, dx$$

  Step 4: Evaluate
    $$= \left[x^2 - \dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_{0}^{2}$$
    $$= \left(4 - \dfrac{8}{3}\right) - (0 - 0)$$
    $$= \dfrac{4}{3} 	ext{ units}^2$$

🔑 Area Between Two Curves
If $f(x) \geq g(x)$ on $[a, b]$:
    $$	ext{Area} = \int_{a}^{b} [f(x) - g(x)] \, dx$$

The limits $a$ and $b$ are the $x$-coordinates where the curves intersect.

💡 Worked Example — Area Between Two Curves
Find the area enclosed by $y = x^2$ and $y = 2x$.

  Step 1: Find intersection points
    $x^2 = 2x$
    $x^2 - 2x = 0$
    $x(x - 2) = 0$
    $x = 0$ or $x = 2$

  Step 2: Determine which curve is on top
    Test $x = 1$: $y_{	ext{line}} = 2$, $y_{	ext{parabola}} = 1$
    So $y = 2x$ is the upper curve on $[0, 2]$

  Step 3: Set up and evaluate
    $$	ext{Area} = \int_{0}^{2} (2x - x^2) \, dx$$
    $$= \left[x^2 - \dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_{0}^{2}$$
    $$= \left(4 - \dfrac{8}{3}\right) - 0$$
    $$= \dfrac{4}{3} 	ext{ units}^2$$

📎 Properties of Definite Integrals
• $\int_{a}^{a} f(x) \, dx = 0$
• $\int_{a}^{b} f(x) \, dx = - \int_{b}^{a} f(x) \, dx$
• $\int_{a}^{b} f(x) \, dx + \int_{b}^{c} f(x) \, dx = \int_{a}^{c} f(x) \, dx$
• $\int_{a}^{b} [f(x) \pm g(x)] \, dx = \int_{a}^{b} f(x) \, dx \pm \int_{a}^{b} g(x) \, dx$

⚠️ Common Mistake
Computing the definite integral without checking whether the curve dips below the $x$-axis. If part of the region is below the axis, that portion contributes a negative value. Always sketch the graph first, find the zeros, and split the integral if needed.

notes.heading: Integration by Substitution
notes.body:
Substitution is the formal method for reversing the chain rule. It is essential when the integrand contains a composite function multiplied by (or closely related to) the derivative of the inner function.

📌 When to Use Substitution
Look for integrands of the form $g'(x) \cdot f(g(x))$. If you can spot the inner function and its derivative, substitution will work.

🔑 The Substitution Method
    1. Choose $u = g(x)$
    2. Find $\dfrac{du}{dx}$ and rearrange to express $dx$ in terms of $du$
    3. Rewrite the entire integral in terms of $u$
    4. Integrate with respect to $u$
    5. Substitute back to $x$

For definite integrals, you can either:
    • Substitute back to $x$ and use the original limits, OR
    • Change the limits to $u$-values and evaluate directly

💡 Worked Example — Indefinite Integral by Substitution
Find $\int 3x^2 \cdot (x^3 + 1)^4 \, dx$.

  Step 1: Choose the substitution
    Let $u = x^3 + 1$

  Step 2: Find $\dfrac{du}{dx}$
    $\dfrac{du}{dx} = 3x^2$
    So $dx = \dfrac{du}{3x^2}$

  Step 3: Rewrite the integral
    $\int 3x^2 \cdot u^4 \cdot \dfrac{du}{3x^2}$
    $= \int u^4 \, du$

  Step 4: Integrate
    $= \dfrac{u^5}{5} + C$

  Step 5: Substitute back
    $= \dfrac{(x^3 + 1)^5}{5} + C$

💡 Worked Example — Definite Integral with Changed Limits
Evaluate $\int_{0}^{1} x \cdot e^{x^2} \, dx$.

  Step 1: Choose $u = x^2$
    $\dfrac{du}{dx} = 2x$, so $dx = \dfrac{du}{2x}$

  Step 2: Change the limits
    When $x = 0$, $u = 0$
    When $x = 1$, $u = 1$

  Step 3: Rewrite and evaluate
    $\int_{0}^{1} x \cdot e^u \cdot \dfrac{du}{2x}$
    $= \int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot e^u \, du$
    $= \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot [e^u]_{0}^{1}$
    $= \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot (e - 1)$

🔑 Special Shortcut — The $\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}$ Pattern
    $$\int \dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)} \, dx = \ln|f(x)| + C$$

This is extremely common in IB exams. Whenever you see a fraction where the numerator looks like the derivative of the denominator, this rule applies.

💡 Worked Example — Using the Shortcut
Find $\int \dfrac{4x - 6}{5 - 3x + x^2} \, dx$.

  Step 1: Check the pattern
    Let $f(x) = 5 - 3x + x^2$
    $f'(x) = -3 + 2x = 2x - 3$
    The numerator is $4x - 6 = 2(2x - 3) = 2f'(x)$

  Step 2: Apply the shortcut
    $= 2 \cdot \int \dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)} \, dx$
    $= 2 \cdot \ln|5 - 3x + x^2| + C$

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Always pick $u$ to be the inner function of a composite expression
• For definite integrals, changing the limits to $u$-values saves time
• If coefficients do not match exactly, use adjust-and-compensate
• The $\ln$ shortcut is just substitution in disguise — spotting it saves steps

⚠️ Common Mistake
Forgetting to change the limits when doing a definite integral by substitution. If you integrate in terms of $u$ but evaluate at $x$-limits, your answer will be wrong. Always convert limits or substitute back before evaluating.

notes.heading: Kinematics and Volume of Revolution
notes.body:
Integration connects the three quantities of motion — displacement, velocity, and acceleration. It also lets us calculate volumes of solids formed by rotating curves around an axis.

📌 Displacement, Velocity, and Acceleration
Differentiation moves downward; integration moves upward:
    $s(t) = 	ext{displacement}$
    $v(t) = \dfrac{ds}{dt} = \int a(t) \, dt + C_1$
    $a(t) = \dfrac{dv}{dt} = \dfrac{d^2s}{dt^2}$

Given different starting information:
• Given $s(t)$: differentiate to get $v(t)$ and $a(t)$
• Given $v(t)$: integrate to get $s(t)$, differentiate to get $a(t)$
• Given $a(t)$: integrate twice to get $v(t)$ then $s(t)$

🔑 Displacement vs Total Distance
    $$	ext{Displacement} = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} v(t) \, dt 	ext{ (signed, net change)}$$
    $$	ext{Total distance} = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} |v(t)| \, dt 	ext{ (always positive)}$$

💡 Worked Example — Total Distance Travelled
A particle moves with velocity $v(t) = t^2 - 4t + 3$ m/s for $0 \leq t \leq 3$. Find the total distance travelled.

  Step 1: Find when velocity changes sign
    $v(t) = (t - 1)(t - 3)$
    $v(t) = 0$ at $t = 1$ and $t = 3$
    Sign diagram: $v > 0$ on $[0, 1)$ and $v < 0$ on $(1, 3]$

  Step 2: Find the antiderivative
    $s(t) = \int v(t) \, dt = \dfrac{t^3}{3} - 2t^2 + 3t + C$
    With $s(0) = 0$, we get $C = 0$

  Step 3: Evaluate displacement at key points
    $s(0) = 0$
    $s(1) = \dfrac{1}{3} - 2 + 3 = \dfrac{4}{3}$
    $s(3) = 9 - 18 + 9 = 0$

  Step 4: Calculate total distance from motion diagram
    $|s(1) - s(0)| + |s(3) - s(1)|$
    $= \dfrac{4}{3} + \dfrac{4}{3}$
    $= \dfrac{8}{3}$ metres

🔑 Volume of Revolution (AA HL)
When the region under $y = f(x)$ from $x = a$ to $x = b$ is rotated $2\pi$ around the $x$-axis:
    $$V = \pi \int_{a}^{b} [f(x)]^2 \, dx$$

When rotating around the $y$-axis, use $x$ as a function of $y$:
    $$V = \pi \int_{a}^{b} [x(y)]^2 \, dy$$

💡 Worked Example — Volume Around the $x$-axis
Find the volume when $y = \sqrt{x}$ from $x = 0$ to $x = 4$ is rotated $2\pi$ about the $x$-axis.

  Step 1: Set up the formula
    $$V = \pi \int_{0}^{4} (\sqrt{x})^2 \, dx$$

  Step 2: Simplify the integrand
    $(\sqrt{x})^2 = x$

  Step 3: Evaluate
    $$V = \pi \int_{0}^{4} x \, dx$$
    $$V = \pi \left[\dfrac{x^2}{2}\right]_{0}^{4}$$
    $$V = \pi \left(\dfrac{16}{2} - 0\right)$$
    $$V = 8\pi 	ext{ cubic units}$$

💡 Worked Example — Volume Around the $y$-axis
The region bounded by $y = x^2$, the $y$-axis, and $y = 4$ is rotated $2\pi$ about the $y$-axis. Find the volume.

  Step 1: Express $x$ in terms of $y$
    $y = x^2$, so $x = \sqrt{y}$

  Step 2: Set up the integral with $y$-limits
    $$V = \pi \int_{0}^{4} (\sqrt{y})^2 \, dy$$
    $$V = \pi \int_{0}^{4} y \, dy$$

  Step 3: Evaluate
    $$V = \pi \left[\dfrac{y^2}{2}\right]_{0}^{4}$$
    $$V = \pi \left(\dfrac{16}{2} - 0\right)$$
    $$V = 8\pi 	ext{ cubic units}$$

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Displacement can be zero while distance is positive (round trips)
• Split at $v = 0$ to compute total distance
• For volume, always square the function before integrating
• Rotation about $y$-axis requires $x$ as a function of $y$
• The $\pi$ factor stays outside the integral

⚠️ Common Mistake
Using displacement instead of total distance when the velocity changes sign. The net displacement can be zero even after travelling a long distance — always check for direction changes by finding where $v(t) = 0$.

notes.heading: Reverse Chain Rule and Composite Functions
notes.body:
The reverse chain rule lets you integrate composite functions by inspection. It is faster than formal substitution when the structure is easy to spot.

📌 Reverse Chain Rule
If $F'(x) = f(x)$, then:
    $$\int g'(x) \cdot f(g(x)) \, dx = F(g(x)) + C$$

In words: if the integrand is the derivative of the inner function times the outer function, the result is the antiderivative of the outer function with the inner function plugged in.

🔑 Linear Composite Functions — Direct Formulas
For any constants $a$ and $b$, with $n 
eq -1$:

    $$\int (ax + b)^n \, dx = \dfrac{(ax + b)^{n+1}}{a(n+1)} + C$$

    $$\int \sin(ax + b) \, dx = -\dfrac{1}{a} \cos(ax + b) + C$$

    $$\int \cos(ax + b) \, dx = \dfrac{1}{a} \sin(ax + b) + C$$

    $$\int \sec^2(ax + b) \, dx = \dfrac{1}{a} 	an(ax + b) + C$$

    $$\int e^{ax + b} \, dx = \dfrac{1}{a} e^{ax + b} + C$$

    $$\int \dfrac{1}{ax + b} \, dx = \dfrac{1}{a} \ln|ax + b| + C$$

💡 Worked Example — Integrating a Linear Composite
Find $\int \sec^2(3x) \, dx$.

  Step 1: Identify the pattern
    This matches $\int \sec^2(ax + b) \, dx$ with $a = 3$, $b = 0$

  Step 2: Apply the formula
    $= \dfrac{1}{3} 	an(3x) + C$

💡 Worked Example — Adjust and Compensate
Find $\int x \cdot (5x^2 - 2)^6 \, dx$.

  Step 1: Spot the inner function
    Let $u = 5x^2 - 2$, then $\dfrac{du}{dx} = 10x$
    We have $x$ in the integrand, but need $10x$

  Step 2: Adjust and compensate
    $x = \dfrac{1}{10} \cdot 10x$
    $	ext{integral} = \dfrac{1}{10} \cdot \int 10x \cdot (5x^2 - 2)^6 \, dx$

  Step 3: Integrate by reverse chain rule
    $= \dfrac{1}{10} \cdot \dfrac{(5x^2 - 2)^7}{7} + C$
    $= \dfrac{(5x^2 - 2)^7}{70} + C$

💡 Worked Example — Definite Integral with Substitution
Evaluate $\int_{1}^{e} \dfrac{1}{x} \, dx$.

  Step 1: Identify the antiderivative
    $$\int \dfrac{1}{x} \, dx = \ln|x| + C$$

  Step 2: Apply the FTC
    $[\ln|x|]_{1}^{e}$
    $= \ln(e) - \ln(1)$
    $= 1 - 0$
    $= 1$

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Every linear composite has a $\dfrac{1}{a}$ factor — do not forget it
• If the inner derivative is present but with a wrong coefficient, adjust and compensate
• For definite integrals with substitution, change limits to $u$-values or substitute back
• Reverse chain rule and substitution are the same idea presented differently

⚠️ Common Mistake
Multiplying by $a$ instead of dividing by $a$. Students often write $\int \sin(4x) \, dx = \cos(4x) + C$, but the correct answer is $-\dfrac{1}{4}\cos(4x) + C$. Always check by differentiating your answer — you should recover the original integrand.

notes.heading: Average Value and Total Change
notes.body:
Definite integrals are not only about area — they also give average values and accumulated totals over an interval.

📌 Definition
The average value of a function $f(x)$ on the interval $[a,b]$ is:
    $$	ext{Average value} = \dfrac{1}{b-a} \int_{a}^{b} f(x) \, dx$$

If $f(x)$ represents a rate of change, the definite integral gives the total change over $[a,b]$.

🔑 Key Concept
Think of the average-value formula as "height $	imes$ width = area, solved for height". The integral gives the signed area under the curve; dividing by the width $b-a$ gives the mean height of the function on that interval.

💡 Worked Example — Average Value
Find the average value of $f(x) = x^2$ on $[0,3]$.

  Step 1: Write the formula
    $$	ext{Average} = \dfrac{1}{3-0} \int_{0}^{3} x^2 \, dx$$

  Step 2: Evaluate the integral
    $$= \dfrac{1}{3} \left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_{0}^{3}$$
    $$= \dfrac{1}{3} \left(\dfrac{27}{3} - 0\right)$$
    $$= \dfrac{1}{3} \cdot 9 = 3$$

💡 Worked Example — Total Change from a Rate
Water flows into a tank at $r(t) = 5 + 2t$ litres per minute for $0 \le t \le 4$. Find the total volume that enters.

  Step 1: Integrate the rate
    $$V = \int_{0}^{4} (5 + 2t) \, dx$$

  Step 2: Evaluate
    $$= \left[5t + t^2\right]_{0}^{4}$$
    $$= (20 + 16) - (0 + 0)$$
    $$= 36 	ext{ litres}$$

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Average value always divides the integral by the length of the interval
• Total change = integral of rate, with appropriate units
• If $f(x)$ is negative on part of the interval, the average value is signed (net average)
• For kinematics, $\int v(t) \, dt$ gives displacement; for flow rates it gives total volume

⚠️ Common Mistake
Forgetting to divide by $b-a$ when asked for an average value. Many students correctly evaluate the integral but then present that as the average.

notes.heading: Integration by Parts
notes.body:
Integration by parts is the reverse of the product rule. It turns a difficult integral into a simpler one.

📌 Definition
For functions $u(x)$ and $v(x)$:
    $$\int u \dfrac{dv}{dx} \, dx = uv - \int v \dfrac{du}{dx} \, dx$$

A compact form is:
    $$\int u \, dv = uv - \int v \, du$$

🔑 How it works
1. Choose $u$ so that its derivative becomes simpler (LIATE: Logarithmic, Inverse trig, Algebraic, Trigonometric, Exponential)
2. Let $dv$ be the rest of the integrand
3. Differentiate $u$ to get $du$
4. Integrate $dv$ to get $v$
5. Substitute into the formula

💡 Worked Example — Polynomial Times Exponential
Find $\int x e^x \, dx$.

  Step 1: Choose $u$ and $dv$
    $u = x$  \quad  $dv = e^x \, dx$

  Step 2: Differentiate and integrate
    $du = dx$  \quad  $v = e^x$

  Step 3: Apply the formula
    $$\int x e^x \, dx = x e^x - \int e^x \, dx$$

  Step 4: Finish
    $$= x e^x - e^x + C$$

💡 Worked Example — Definite Integral by Parts
Evaluate $\int_{0}^{1} x e^x \, dx$.

  Using the antiderivative from above:
    $$\left[x e^x - e^x\right]_{0}^{1}$$
    $$= (1 \cdot e - e) - (0 - 1)$$
    $$= 1$$

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Pick $u$ using LIATE to make the new integral simpler
• Sometimes integration by parts must be applied more than once (e.g. $x^2 e^x$)
• For definite integrals, evaluate $uv$ and the remaining integral at both limits
• The constant $C$ is only added at the very end

⚠️ Common Mistake
Choosing the wrong $u$. If we had set $u = e^x$ in $\int x e^x \, dx$, the integral would become harder, not easier. Always differentiate the part that simplifies.

notes.heading: 💡 Worked Example — Kinematics with Variable Acceleration
notes.body:
When acceleration is not constant, integration is needed to move from acceleration to velocity and then to displacement. This worked example shows how to handle a sign change in velocity when finding total distance.

📌 Problem
A particle starts from rest and moves in a straight line with acceleration $a(t) = 6t - 12$ m/s${}^2$ for $0 \le t \le 5$. Find the total distance travelled during the first 5 seconds.

🔑 Strategy
1. Integrate $a(t)$ to obtain $v(t)$, using $v(0) = 0$ to find the constant.
2. Find the times when $v(t) = 0$, because these are the points where the particle changes direction.
3. Integrate $|v(t)|$ piecewise, or evaluate displacement at the turning points and add absolute changes.

💡 Solution
Step 1: Find the velocity function.
    $v(t) = \int (6t - 12) \, dt = 3t^2 - 12t + C$
    Since $v(0) = 0$, we get $C = 0$, so $v(t) = 3t^2 - 12t = 3t(t - 4)$.

Step 2: Locate direction changes.
    $v(t) = 0$ at $t = 0$ and $t = 4$.
    The velocity is negative on $(0, 4)$ and positive on $(4, 5]$.

Step 3: Find the displacement function.
    $s(t) = \int v(t) \, dt = t^3 - 6t^2 + C$
    With $s(0) = 0$, $C = 0$, so $s(t) = t^3 - 6t^2$.

Step 4: Evaluate at the key times.
    $s(0) = 0$
    $s(4) = 64 - 96 = -32$ metres
    $s(5) = 125 - 150 = -25$ metres

Step 5: Add the absolute distances between turning points.
    Total distance $= |s(4) - s(0)| + |s(5) - s(4)|$
    $= |-32 - 0| + |-25 - (-32)|$
    $= 32 + 7 = 39$ metres

📎 Key Takeaway
Total distance requires $|v(t)|$, not just $v(t)$. Whenever velocity changes sign, split the interval at the zeros and add the positive contributions.

questions.stem: Which statement about integration is NOT always true?
choices: $\int x \cdot f(x) \, dx = x \cdot \int f(x) \, dx$
$\int k \cdot f(x) \, dx = k \cdot \int f(x) \, dx$
questions.explanation: Integration distributes over addition and constant multiplication, but NOT over multiplication. The integral of a product is not the product of the integrals. This is a common misconception-there is no simple reverse of the product rule.
$f(x) = 2x^3 - 2x^2 + C$. Using $f(1)=3$: $3 = 2-2+C \Rightarrow C=3$. So $f(2)=16-8+3=11$. Choice $8$ comes from forgetting $+C$; choice $5$ from an arithmetic error in finding $C$.

$\int \sec^2(ax) \, dx = \dfrac{1}{a}	an(ax) + C$. Here $a=3$, so divide by $3$. Choice $A$ forgets the $\dfrac{1}{a}$ factor; choice $C$ multiplies by $a$ instead; choice $D$ ignores the $3x$ entirely.

questions.stem: Find the area enclosed by $y = x^2$ and $y = 2x$.
questions.explanation: Intersection at $x=0$ and $x=2$. $	ext{Area} = \int_{0}^{2} (2x - x^2) \, dx = \left[x^2 - \dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_{0}^{2} = 4 - \dfrac{8}{3} = \dfrac{4}{3}$. Choice $B$ is the area under the line only; choice $C$ integrates the wrong function; choice $D$ has a sign error.

questions.explanation: $V = \pi \int_{0}^{4} x^2 \, dy = \pi \int_{0}^{4} y \, dy = \pi \left[\dfrac{y^2}{2}\right]_{0}^{4} = 8\pi$. Choice $B$ is what you get if you mistakenly rotate about the $x$-axis ($\pi \int_{0}^{2} (x^2)^2 \, dx = \dfrac{32\pi}{5}$). Choice $C$ forgets the $\dfrac{1}{2}$ from integration.

questions.stem: A particle moves with velocity $v(t) = t^2 - 4t + 3$ m/s for $0 \leq t \leq 3$. Find the total distance travelled.
questions.explanation: $v(t) = (t-1)(t-3)$, so $v>0$ on $[0,1)$ and $v<0$ on $(1,3]$. Split the integral: $\int_{0}^{1} (t^2-4t+3) \, dt + \int_{1}^{3} -(t^2-4t+3) \, dt = \dfrac{4}{3} + \dfrac{4}{3} = \dfrac{8}{3}$. Choice $B$ is the displacement (net zero); choice $C$ only counts the first interval; choice $D$ has a sign error.

questions.stem: Find the average value of $f(x) = x^2$ on the interval $[0,3]$.
questions.explanation: Average value = $\dfrac{1}{3-0} \int_{0}^{3} x^2 \, dx = \dfrac{1}{3} \left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_{0}^{3} = \dfrac{1}{3} \cdot 9 = 3$.
Using integration by parts with $u=x$ and $dv=e^x dx$: $\int x e^x \, dx = x e^x - \int e^x \, dx = x e^x - e^x + C$.

questions.stem: Water flows into a tank at $r(t) = 5 + 2t$ litres per minute for $0 \le t \le 4$. Find the total volume that enters.

questions.explanation: Use the substitution $u = x + 1$, so $x = u - 1$ and $dx = du$. The limits change from $x = 0$ to $u = 1$ and from $x = 3$ to $u = 4$. The integral becomes $\int_{1}^{4} \dfrac{u - 1}{\sqrt{u}} \, du = \int_{1}^{4} (u^{1/2} - u^{-1/2}) \, du$. Evaluating gives $\left[\dfrac{2}{3}u^{3/2} - 2u^{1/2}\right]_{1}^{4} = \left(\dfrac{16}{3} - 4\right) - \left(\dfrac{2}{3} - 2\right) = \dfrac{8}{3}$.

questions.stem: The finite region bounded by $y = x^2$ and $y = 2x$ is rotated $2\pi$ about the $x$-axis. Find the volume of revolution.
questions.explanation: The curves intersect where $x^2 = 2x$, giving $x = 0$ and $x = 2$. On $[0, 2]$ the line $y = 2x$ is above the parabola $y = x^2$, so use the washer method: $V = \pi \int_{0}^{2} [(2x)^2 - (x^2)^2] \, dx = \pi \int_{0}^{2} (4x^2 - x^4) \, dx$. This evaluates to $\pi \left[\dfrac{4x^3}{3} - \dfrac{x^5}{5}\right]_{0}^{2} = \pi \left(\dfrac{32}{3} - \dfrac{32}{5}\right) = \dfrac{64\pi}{15}$.

questions.stem: A particle moves with acceleration $a(t) = 2t - 6$ m/s${}^2$. Its initial velocity is $8$ m/s. Find the total distance travelled in the first $5$ seconds.
questions.explanation: First integrate acceleration: $v(t) = \int (2t - 6) \, dt = t^2 - 6t + 8$, using $v(0) = 8$ to fix the constant as $8$. Factorising gives $v(t) = (t - 2)(t - 4)$, so the velocity changes sign at $t = 2$ and $t = 4$. The displacement is $s(t) = \dfrac{t^3}{3} - 3t^2 + 8t$. Evaluating at $0, 2, 4, 5$ yields $0, \dfrac{20}{3}, \dfrac{16}{3}, \dfrac{20}{3}$. The total distance is $\left|\dfrac{20}{3}\right| + \left|\dfrac{16}{3} - \dfrac{20}{3}\right| + \left|\dfrac{20}{3} - \dfrac{16}{3}\right| = \dfrac{20}{3} + \dfrac{4}{3} + \dfrac{4}{3} = \dfrac{28}{3}$ metres.

This requires integration by parts twice. First set $u = x^2$ and $dv = e^x dx$, giving $du = 2x dx$ and $v = e^x$, so $\int x^2 e^x dx = x^2 e^x - 2\int x e^x dx$. For the remaining integral use parts again with $u = x$ and $dv = e^x dx$ to get $\int x e^x dx = x e^x - e^x$. Substituting back gives $x^2 e^x - 2x e^x + 2e^x + C = e^x(x^2 - 2x + 2) + C$.

questions.stem: Find the total area enclosed by the curve $y = x^3 - x$ and the $x$-axis.
questions.explanation: The curve cuts the $x$-axis where $x^3 - x = 0$, so $x(x - 1)(x + 1) = 0$ and the intersections are $x = -1, 0, 1$. The curve is below the axis on $[0, 1]$ and above on $[-1, 0]$. By symmetry the total area is $2\int_{0}^{1} [0 - (x^3 - x)] \, dx = 2\int_{0}^{1} (x - x^3) \, dx$. Evaluating gives $2\left[\dfrac{x^2}{2} - \dfrac{x^4}{4}\right]_{0}^{1} = 2\left(\dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{4}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}$.
